sens: Son of Boaz and Ruth
Father of Jesse and grandfather of King David
G5601.detail: Obed is a character from the Old Testament, son of Boaz and Ruth (Matthew 1:5). He is the father of Jesse and the grandfather of King David, holding an important place in the royal genealogy of Israel (Luke 3:32). His name means "servant" in Hebrew, which evokes a humble position, even though he is an ancestor of the greatest king of Israel.
G5601.origine: The name Obed comes from the Hebrew עוֹבֵד (ʿôbēd), which literally means "servant" or "one who serves." It is formed from the root עבד (ʿabad), which means "to serve." This name reveals a certain humility of the character, contrasting with his royal lineage: a servant whose lineage produces the kings of Israel and, according to Christian faith, the Messiah.
G5601.emploi: Obed appears twice in the New Testament, always in genealogies. Matthew 1:5 mentions him as the fruit of the union between Boaz and Ruth, a union that seals Ruth's story and confirms her place in David's family. Luke 3:32 places him in the genealogical line of Jesus, showing how the Messiah descends from this remarkable union. These two passages establish his role as a crucial link in the generational chain leading to David and Christ.
G5601.portee: The presence of Obed in the genealogies of Jesus reminds Christians that God works in the ordinary history of men, often through humble figures and unexpected situations. The union of Boaz and Ruth, from which Obed is born, is an example of God's design that includes even outsiders and the marginalized in the lineage of the Messiah. This genealogy invites the reader to see how God directs events toward His salvific purpose.

sens: In this place, at this specific location
Toward this place, in this direction
In this circumstance, in this context
G5602.detail:
1. The primary and most common meaning: "here" designates the place where the speaker is or wants to show. Jesus asks the father of the demon-possessed boy: "Bring your son here" (Luke 9:41), pointing to the place where he stands. Peter confesses: "It is good for us to be here" on the Mount of Transfiguration (Mark 9:5), rejoicing to be in this place with Jesus.
2. The movement toward this place: "here" can also mean "toward this place." When the disciples ask Jesus, "Have you come here to torment us before the time?" (Matthew 8:29), they refer to His coming to this place, His presence among them.
3. Figuratively, "here" designates the context or circumstance of the moment. Paul writes: "Moreover, it is required in stewards that one be found faithful. But with me, it is a very small thing that I should be judged by you or by a human court; in fact, I do not even judge myself" (1 Corinthians 4:2). The word then points to the situation or issue of the moment, not a geographical location.
G5602.origine: The Greek word ὧδε (hōde) is an ancient adverb of place, whose form is related to the same family as the demonstrative "this/that." In Hebrew and Aramaic of the Old Testament, Greek translators rendered words like פֹּה ("here") and חֲלֹם ("there") with ὧδε, as well as the interjection הִנֶּה ("behold"). The word expresses the idea of proximity and immediate presence.
G5602.emploi: ὧδε appears 59 times in the New Testament, mostly in the Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke, John). It is first used concretely to designate a specific place: where Jesus stands, where objects are gathered, where events occur. We see it in "the loaves are not lacking here" (Mark 8:4), or "all the dead that are taken away from here" (Luke 17:23). Gradually, it takes on a more abstract or argumentative meaning: "Something greater than the temple is here" (Matthew 12:6) speaks of the presence of Jesus as a spiritual reality. In Revelation, it is used to emphasize a truth or judgment that imposes itself at the moment of speech.
G5602.portee: This small word reminds us of the physical reality of Christ: Jesus is not an abstraction; He came "here," in flesh, in a specific place, at a precise moment in history. For the believer, "here" invites recognition of God's concrete presence in the current circumstances of life, not in a distant elsewhere or in a flight from reality.

sens: Song or hymn, particularly a musical composition intended to be sung
Song of praise addressed to God or Christ
New or exceptional song expressing joy and adoration
Spiritual song that edifies and instructs the assembly of believers
G5603.detail:
1. A cantique is primarily a song or musical composition of a solemn nature: it can be sung alone or in a group, and it contrasts with simple recited words. In Revelation 5:9, the heavenly creatures "sang a new cantique," which shows that it is performed vocally before an assembly.
2. In the Bible, every cantique is a praise directed toward God or Christ. It is never a secular or worldly song, but always an expression of worship and gratitude toward the Lord. Revelation 15:3 is a perfect illustration: it sings "the cantique of Moses" and "the cantique of the Lamb." 
3. Revelation mentions several times a "new cantique": it is a song composed to celebrate a new act of God, particularly redemption through Christ (Revelation 5:9). This "newness" expresses wonder and joy in the face of recently accomplished divine works.
4. Spiritual cantiques serve a function in the life of the Church: they educate, exhort, and edify believers. In Ephesians 5:19 and Colossians 3:16, Paul invites Christians to speak to one another "in psalms, hymns, and spiritual cantiques," which shows that singing serves mutual instruction and encouragement in faith.
G5603.origine: The word ᾠδή (ōdē) comes from ancient Greek and designates any form of song. In Hebrew, it primarily corresponds to שִׁיר (shir), the common word for "song" or "chant." The Greek word is related to the root meaning "to sing" (ἀείδω). In the Greek Old Testament, this word regularly translates the psalms and songs of Israelite praise, which explains why in the New Testament it is always used for religious songs and not secular ones.
G5603.emploi: The word appears five times in the New Testament, always in a context of divine praise. Three occurrences are found in Revelation (5:9; 14:3; 15:3), where John describes the heavenly songs of creatures and the redeemed before the throne of God. Two occurrences are in the Pauline epistles (Ephesians 5:19; Colossians 3:16), where the apostle exhorts the churches to use spiritual cantiques as a means of mutual edification. In Revelation, the cantique is often referred to as "new" (5:9; 14:3), which emphasizes its connection to eschatological fulfillment. Paul places it alongside "psalms" and "hymns," three complementary poetic genres for the prayer and worship life of the Church.
G5603.portee: The cantique reminds us that the worship of God is not a solitary or purely mental activity, but a communal, joyful, and bodily expression. For the Christian, learning to sing the spiritual cantique is to align one's voice and heart with the great hymn of praise raised by the heavens themselves. It also recognizes that religious music has a particular power to edify faith and unite the assembly in a shared love for the Lord. The word invites us not to separate reason and emotion in our worship: the cantique engages the whole being.

sens: The sufferings that accompany childbirth
Agony and extreme anguish
The sufferings that herald a serious or catastrophic event
G5604.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to the pains of labor during childbirth: this is the most direct physical meaning. In 1 Thessalonians 5:3, Paul compares the sudden arrival of judgment to the pains that seize a pregnant woman — unavoidable, intense, and heralding something serious.
2. The word extends to any extreme suffering or agony. In Acts 2:24, the "pangs of death" are called ôdin: it is the anguish and distress of death itself. This is why the word evokes not only physical pain but also the moral oppression that accompanies it.
3. In a figurative and apocalyptic sense, ôdin refers to the sufferings that precede and announce great upheavals. In Matthew 24:8 and Mark 13:8, earthquakes, famines, and wars of the end times are called the "birth pains": like a woman in labor, these signs only announce the greater event that is coming.
G5604.origine: The Greek word ôdin comes from an ancient root that expresses the idea of contraction and tightening. It corresponds in Hebrew to several terms: חֶבֶל (ḥevel, "cord," "rope") and חִיל (ḥil, "anguish"). The image is that of the body contracting and tightening under pain — both physically and morally. It is a word that paints the reality of suffering, not just its abstract notion.
G5604.emploi: The word appears 4 times in the New Testament, always in serious contexts. Matthew and Mark use it together to speak of the signs of the end: natural and social disasters are like the premonitory pains of the new world. Paul in 1 Thessalonians 5:3 uses it in the same way: judgment will surprise careless men like a woman in labor. In Acts 2:24, Peter describes the resurrection of Christ as a deliverance "from the pangs of death" — this rare term for death itself reinforces the idea of an oppression from which one needed to escape. In all these passages, ôdin expresses not only pain but also the anguish and inevitability of what is to come.
G5604.portee: This word reminds Christians that pain and suffering are never without meaning in God's plan. Just as birth pains herald a new life, the sufferings of the world and the Church announce the coming of the Lord and the end of all distress. It is an invitation to vigilance and hope: not to sleep spiritually in the face of the signs, but to maintain the assurance that God is guiding history toward its fulfillment.

sens: To experience the pains of childbirth, to be in labor during a birth
To suffer intensely as in the pains of childbirth
To be in anxious anticipation of something that is to be born or realized
G5605.detail:
1. The primary meaning is physical: to experience the contractions and pains that accompany childbirth. A pregnant woman "gives birth" when she is in labor before delivering (Revelation 12:2: "she cried out in labor and in the pains of childbirth").
2. By extension, the word describes any intense, ongoing, and inevitable suffering, like that of birth pains. It is an image of the effort and hardship one endures.
3. In a figurative sense, Paul uses this word to express his spiritual anxiety: he "experiences again the pains of childbirth" as he waits for Christ to be formed in his spiritual children (Galatians 4:19). This evokes worry, inner tension, and the continuous effort to see something essential born in others.
G5605.origine: The Greek word ὠδίνω comes from an ancient root that designates the pains of childbirth. In Hebrew, it often translates the verb חוּל (houl), which first means "to turn around," then "to writhe in pain." The word is linked to the idea of torment, of violent movement of the body under suffering. The root image is that of contractions and uncontrollable movements of the body during labor.
G5605.emploi: The word appears three times in the New Testament, all in Pauline epistles and Revelation. In Revelation 12:2, it literally describes a pregnant woman crying out under the pains of childbirth. In Galatians 4:27, it evokes the pains of one who has given birth (a quotation from Isaiah). But the richest usage is found in Galatians 4:19, where Paul transfers this image to the spiritual realm: he speaks of his own apostolic sufferings as "birth pains." This metaphor emphasizes the intensity, continuity, and inevitability of his pastoral efforts to form Christ in his converts. The verb thus expresses both real physical pain and spiritual inner suffering.
G5605.portee: For the believer, this word reveals that spiritual growth comes at a cost. Paul does not hesitate to show his vulnerability: he truly suffers while waiting for the maturation of his brothers in Christ. This teaches that spiritual childbirth—forming Christ in ourselves or in others—requires work, patience, and a certain pain. It is an invitation to recognize that all true transformation is born of effort and perseverance, and that those who accompany others in their growth in Christ participate in a noble and fruitful suffering.

sens: Part of the human body between the neck and the arm
Area of the body capable of bearing a burden
Symbol of strength or capacity to support
G5606.detail:
1. The shoulder is the fleshy part of the body that connects the neck to the arm. It is an important joint for all movements of the arms and hands.
2. The shoulder is the place where one places a burden to carry it: the scribes and Pharisees imposed heavy loads on the shoulders of people (Matthew 23:4), while the shepherd in the parable puts the found sheep on his shoulders to bring it home (Luke 15:5).
3. The shoulder can represent someone's ability to bear a load, to support a weight or responsibility, making it an image of strength or dedication.
G5606.origine: The Greek word ὦμος comes from an Indo-European root designating the joints of the body. In Hebrew, the word translated here is שְׁכֶם (šékèm), which literally means "shoulder" and has given its name to the city of Shechem (Schekèm), built between two mountains like between two shoulders. The word always evokes the physical capacity to carry or support.
G5606.emploi: The word appears only twice in the preserved New Testament. In Matthew 23:4, Jesus reproaches the Pharisees for loading people with heavy observances without bearing the weight themselves. In Luke 15:5, the joyful shepherd carries the lost sheep on his shoulders to bring it back to the fold. These two scenes — one showing an unjust burden imposed on others, the other showing an act of tenderness and care — give the word its dual moral and spiritual significance.
G5606.portee: The shoulder reminds us that those in authority have the duty to share the weight they impose, not to aggravate it. It also illustrates the joy of the shepherd who cares for each of his sheep and does not hesitate to bear the burden himself to bring them back. It is a powerful image of Christ's mercy toward His own.

sens: acquire something in exchange for money
obtain through payment
G5608.detail: 1. To buy means to give money in exchange for something in return. In Acts 7:16, Abraham bought a tomb from the sons of Hemor by paying a sum of money; this is a land purchase, an ordinary business transaction. 2. Figuratively, the word can also express the idea of acquiring or obtaining something through a price or exchange, but this figurative use does not clearly appear in the Greek New Testament.
G5608.origine: The Greek verb comes from an ancient root denoting exchange and sale. It is related to the notion of purchase or commercial acquisition. In classical Greek, the term 'priamai' (to buy) was more commonly used, but 'ōneomai' is an older or dialectal form that carries the same meaning. This verb simply expresses the concrete action of buying: giving money to receive a good.
G5608.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 7:16. Peter recounts the story of Abraham who bought a tomb from the sons of Hemor to bury his people. It is a historical account reporting a real commercial transaction: Abraham paid a sum of money to acquire this burial ground. The usage is strictly historical and narrative; the word simply describes the action of buying without any particular theological nuance.
G5608.portee: This word reminds us that the patriarchs acted in the real world, concluding business and contracts. It shows that Abraham, although a man of faith, also performed ordinary acts of life: buying land, organizing burials. This anchors biblical faith in concrete history and human relationships.

sens: Oval object produced by a hen or a bird
Simple and nutritious food, symbol of the natural and expected gift
G5609.detail:
1. The word refers to the egg as we know it: the oval object laid by a hen or a bird, which contains a germ of life. In Luke 11:12, Jesus uses it as an example of a simple and natural thing that a father would give to his son who asks for it. It is a basic food, accessible to all, that could be easily found in Palestine.
2. By extension, the egg symbolizes the expected gift, the normal and safe good. Jesus contrasts it with the scorpion—a harmful and venomous creature—to illustrate the absurdity of a father giving harm to his child. The image emphasizes trust: a father never deceives his son by reversing good and evil.
G5609.origine: The Greek word ōon comes from an ancient root common to several Indo-European languages to denote the egg. The Hebrew word beitsa (בֵּיצָה), which has the same etymological root, is rendered by this Greek term in the Septuagint (Greek translation of the Old Testament). The word simply expresses the biological reality: the product of the hen, a source of life.
G5609.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 11:12. Jesus uses it in his teaching on prayer and trust in God the Father. He argues from common sense: if a child asks for food, his father will not give him a disguised harmful food (an egg disguised as a scorpion). This contrast between the harmless egg and the deadly scorpion illustrates that God never misleads those who sincerely ask Him. The context is one of assurance that God responds to the legitimate requests of His children.
G5609.portee: This word reinforces the message that God is good and reliable. Jesus calls us to trust: our legitimate requests do not receive traps or deception from our heavenly Father. The simple image of the egg reminds us that God knows our basic needs and responds to them with kindness, never reversing good and evil. It is a call to abandon our fears and to ask with confidence.

sens: a division of day and night, a duration of sixty minutes
a precise moment or instant in time
the opportune moment, the decisive moment, the occasion
a period or season set by nature
G5610.detail:
1. The hour is primarily a measure of time: the twelve hours of day and the twelve hours of night. In Matthew 20:3-9, we see workers hired at different hours of the day, which shows how the word designates the concrete divisions of the day. In Matthew 26:40, Jesus asks Peter to watch "for one hour" with Him, a precise duration.
2. Hour also means an instant, a particular moment in time. In Luke 2:38, Simeon arrives "at that very hour" when Jesus is presented at the temple. In Acts 22:13, Paul regains his sight "at that moment," at the exact time when Ananias speaks to him.
3. Especially in John, "hour" takes on a deeper meaning: it is the moment that God has set, the decisive moment. When Jesus tells His mother in John 2:4, "My hour has not yet come," He is referring to the hour of His death and glorification, the moment assigned to Him by the Father. In John 12:23, "The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified": this is the moment of destiny, planned by God.
4. More rarely, hour designates a season or natural period, as seen in Ecclesiastes or ancient Greek authors, but this meaning is less frequent in the New Testament.
G5610.origine: The Greek word ὥρα comes from an ancient root that evokes what is "delimited" or "marked." In Hebrew and Aramaic, this word is often translated by עֵת ("opportune moment") or שָׁעָה ("hour"). The word has retained its concrete meaning of division of time, but in the Gospels, especially in John, it enriches itself with a theological dimension: it is the moment intended by God, the moment of the fulfillment of the divine plan.
G5610.emploi: The word ὥρα appears about a hundred times in the New Testament, very frequently in the Gospels and Acts. In Matthew and Mark, it often designates a concrete division of the day (Matthew 20:3-12, Mark 15:25: "the third hour") or a duration of watch (Matthew 26:40). In Luke, it marks precise and important moments in the life of Jesus or the early Church. In John, the word takes on a particular depth: the "hour" becomes the decisive moment intended by God, notably the hour of Jesus' death and resurrection (John 2:4, 12:23, 13:1, 17:1). In John 4:21-23 and 5:25, the "hour" is that of worship in spirit and truth, of the judgment of the dead. Paul also uses it to mark critical moments (1 Corinthians 4:11, Romans 13:11).
G5610.portee: This word teaches us that our life flows in time, divided into instants and moments. But for the Christian, the "hour" is never just a blind succession of seconds: each moment can be God's hour, the moment when He acts and calls us. Jesus teaches us that certain hours are decisive, filled with divine significance. This invites the reader to take the present seriously, to recognize the moments when God acts in their life, and to live each day as part of God's eternal plan.

sens: Pleasing to the eye, having an attractive appearance
In good condition, well presented, neat
Timely, occurring at the right moment
(Figuratively) Having an attractive exterior that conceals a hidden reality
G5611.detail:
1. This word primarily describes what is beautiful, pleasant to look at: in Acts 3:2 and 3:10, the "Beautiful" gate of the temple is one that has a beautiful architectural and artistic appearance.
2. The word also applies to what is well presented or neat: the tombs in Matthew 23:27 appear "beautiful" on the outside because they are whitewashed, thus clean and shiny.
3. The original image of the Greek word refers to something that is ripe, blossoming, at its best moment — what happens at its opportune time. In Romans 10:15, the "beautiful" feet of those who announce peace evoke a timely and welcome arrival.
4. Matthew 23:27 reveals a critical nuance: being "beautiful" can mask a repulsive reality, a false appearance of purity.
G5611.origine: The word comes from the Greek root *hōra* ("hour," "season"). The basic image is that of fruit coming to maturity, of a flower blooming at the right time. Hence: what pleases because it is at its best state, flourishing, in full season. The Greek uses this word to translate several Hebrew words from the Old Testament that express beauty or what is good.
G5611.emploi: The word appears four times in the New Testament. In Acts 3:2 and 3:10, it refers to the Beautiful Gate of the Jerusalem temple, famous for its architectural beauty. In Matthew 23:27, Jesus uses it critically: the tombs "appear beautiful" on the outside, but contain death — this is the only usage where beauty conceals an ugly truth. In Romans 10:15 (quoting Isaiah), "beautiful" describes the feet of the messenger who brings good news, where beauty expresses rather the opportunity and appeal of the awaited coming.
G5611.portee: This word reminds us that appearance can be deceptive: it does not reveal the truth of what is inside. For the believer, Jesus' warning in Matthew 23 invites us to look beyond external seduction, to seek inner purity. Conversely, the beauty of the feet of the apostle who brings the Gospel shows that true beauty lies in what brings peace and good news.

sens: To make a powerful and threatening cry (animal)
To produce a loud and terrifying voice
To manifest a threat with force and noise
G5612.detail:
1. The verb describes the characteristic cry of the lion and some fierce animals — this deep, loud, and terrifying growl they emit to mark their territory or intimidate. It is a very concrete image: one can almost hear the roar.
2. Figuratively, to roar applies to a threat that manifests loudly, dangerously, in a way that is heard and feared. The devil in 1 Peter 5:8 is described as a "roaring lion": this image paints an adversary who does not hide his evil intentions, who openly threatens, seeking to frighten by his mere presence and noise.
G5612.origine: The verb ὠρύομαι (ōruomai) is an ancient Greek verb, formed from a root that reproduces the noise itself — an onomatopoeia. The biblical context shows it rendering the Hebrew שָׁאַג (shaag), which has exactly the same meaning: the roar of the lion, this natural and terrifying cry. This sound etymology reminds us that the word imitates what it describes.
G5612.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Peter 5:8, where Peter exhorts believers to be vigilant. He characterizes the devil with an image of brutal and overt animal threat. The apostle does not speak of a hidden or sneaky threat, but of a danger that makes itself known by its noise and fury — like a predator that prowls without fear. This choice of the word "roar" intensifies the urgency of the warning: the threat is loud, visible, imminent.
G5612.portee: This image of the roaring lion reminds the believer that evil does not always proceed in silence or only by cunning: it also manifests itself through a loud and threatening power. The exhortation to "be watchful" and remain "sober" takes on its full meaning in the face of an open threat. The roar of the lion is there to wake us up, not to paralyze us: it is a call to vigilance, not to panic.

sens: In the same way as, according to the manner in which
Approximately, about
At the moment when, when
In order that, so that
According to opinion or appearance
G5613.detail:
1. The most common meaning: one compares two situations or two ways of acting. One says "as" to show that one thing resembles another or is done in the same way. Example: "Love your neighbor as yourself" (Matthew 22:39) — you must love him in the same way you love yourself.
2. In front of a number, "as" means "about" or "approximately": it does not give an exact figure, but an approximation. Example: "There were about two thousand pigs" (Mark 5:13).
3. Time: "as" can mean "when" or "at the moment when" something happens. Example: "It happened that, when Elizabeth heard the greeting of Mary" (Luke 1:41).
4. Intention or purpose: "as" sometimes introduces an action done to accomplish something. Example: "Jesus sent messengers to prepare a lodging for him" (Luke 9:52).
5. Finally, "as" can mean "according to what appears" or "according to people's opinion" — it is appearance, not reality. Example: "Not as lording it over those entrusted to you" (1 Peter 5:3) — do not govern only by giving this impression.
G5613.origine: The Greek word ὡς comes from the same root as the relative pronoun "who." Originally, it is a form of relative adverb: it serves to show the link, the resemblance, or the manner. In Hebrew, the corresponding word is often כַּ (ka), which means "as" or "according to." This small, very ancient, and very frequent word is one of the essential connectors in Greek for expressing comparison and time.
G5613.emploi: This word is among the most frequent in the New Testament: it appears more than 450 times. It is found in all four Gospels and in the epistles, always with the same role: to establish a resemblance, a comparison, or a relationship of time. In the Gospels, Jesus constantly uses it to teach by comparison ("as a grain of mustard seed"). In the epistles, Paul and Peter use it to explain how to behave ("as" beloved children, or "as" Moses). Its usage extends from simple comparison to finer nuances: approximation, time, intended purpose, and even opinion.
G5613.portee: This small word shows us how the Bible often teaches by analogy and comparison. When Jesus says "be perfect as your heavenly Father is perfect" (Matthew 5:48), this word brings us back to the divine example. Understanding the nuances of "as" helps us grasp whether the Bible speaks of a real resemblance, a mere appearance, or a goal to be achieved. It is a humble yet powerful word for following Christ: "be like children" (Matthew 18:3).

sens: Cry of acclamation and supplication addressed to Jesus
Expression of a request for salvation or help
Praise and blessing to the one who comes in the name of the Lord
G5614.detail:
1. Hosanna is a cry of acclamation that the crowd shouts during Jesus' triumphant entry into Jerusalem. The people who go before and follow Jesus shout "Hosanna to the Son of David" (Matthew 21:9), which expresses a joyful welcome and solemn recognition.
2. The word also carries a dimension of supplication or a call for help, as it literally means "save now." When the children shout "Hosanna to the Son of David" in the temple (Matthew 21:15), they express both their joy and their expectation that Jesus will save them.
3. Hosanna is a blessing addressed to the one who comes in the name of the Lord, often associated with the words "Blessed is he who comes" (John 12:13). It is a liturgical cry that recognizes Jesus as God's messenger.
G5614.origine: Hosanna comes from Hebrew and literally means "save now" or "please, save us." It is derived from two words: "hôshîa'" (to save) and "nâ'" (I pray, please). It was a common liturgical exclamation in Israelite worship, particularly used during festivals, especially at the Feast of Tabernacles. The Greeks transliterated it without translating it, preserving this cry as a sacred and traditional expression.
G5614.emploi: Hosanna appears only five times in the New Testament, exclusively in the accounts of Jesus' triumphant entry into Jerusalem, found in the first three Gospels and in John. In Matthew 21:9 and 21:15, it is accompanied by "to the Son of David," reinforcing the messianic recognition. In Mark 11:9-10, the cry "Hosanna" frames a blessing on the reign of David. John 12:13 explicitly connects it to the one "who comes in the name of the Lord." Everywhere, it is a joyful acclamation but also a supplication, transforming the cry into a recognition of Jesus' saving authority.
G5614.portee: Hosanna invites us to recognize that crying out to Jesus is both praising him and asking for his help. This word reminds us that the Christian faith is expressed in strong, public, and confident words. By giving us access to this cry of the crowd in Jerusalem, Scripture calls us to welcome Jesus as the one who saves, with the same fervor and certainty.

sens: In the same way, identically
Also, too
Likewise (for people or things)
G5615.detail:
1. In the same way, identically: the word expresses a repetition or exact resemblance. In Matthew 20:5, the employer "went out again at the sixth hour and at the ninth, and he did likewise" — meaning he called workers as before. It is an action that is reproduced.

2. Also, too: the word can simply add something to what has already been said, without insisting on perfect identity. In Luke 13:5, "if you do not repent, you will all likewise perish" — all without exception will suffer the same fate.

3. Likewise (for people or things): when several beings or facts are parallel. In Mark 12:21, after the death of the second son, "it was the same for the third" — the third lived exactly like the second. At the table, in 1 Corinthians 11:25, the Lord "took likewise the cup, after having supped" — he reproduced the gesture he had made with the bread.
G5615.origine: The word is formed from ὡς ("as," "thus") reinforced by αὔτως ("in the same way"), hence "in this same manner." It is a common word in biblical Greek, modeled on Hebrew idiom, to create parallels or to show that an action is repeated identically.
G5615.emploi: The word appears 17 times in the New Testament, mostly in the Gospels and Paul's epistles. It serves to establish a parallel or a repetition: either an identical action (Matthew 20:5, 21:30), or a resemblance between several people or situations (Mark 12:21 for the three sons). Sometimes the verb is implied and must be found in the previous sentence (Luke 22:20: "he took likewise the cup" refers back to the gesture with the bread). In the pastoral epistles (1 Timothy, Titus), it enumerates behaviors or duties that are added: "likewise the women must be dignified" (1 Timothy 3:11).
G5615.portee: This small word invites the reader to look at the repetitions and parallels in biblical history: it shows how God acts according to constant principles, and how his requirements apply to all. By rereading the passages where it appears, we see that God treats his servants with the same justice, and that he requires the same obedience from us.

sens: In the same way as, similarly to
Approximately, about (with a number)
That has the appearance of, that resembles
G5616.detail:
1. The word expresses a comparison: it establishes that two things are similar or act in a similar manner. In Matthew 3:16, the Spirit descends "like" a dove: it is the image of a gentle and peaceful descent. In Luke 22:44, Jesus' sweat falls "like" drops of blood: it is a striking comparison of his physical agony.
2. When it comes to numbers, the word indicates an approximation, not an exact quantity. In Luke 9:14, there were "about" five thousand men: the figure is given without claiming precision. Similarly, in Acts 2:41, about three thousand souls were baptized. It is an honest way of counting what cannot be measured exactly.
3. The word can express how something seems or appears to be. In Luke 24:11, the women report dreams that the disciples consider "as" dreams, meaning they judge them to be vain. Appearance takes precedence over reality.
G5616.origine: The word comes from a Greek root meaning "similar" or "comparable." It carries the idea of resemblance and approximation. It is a very flexible adverb, functioning as a particle of comparison or mitigation: it never says "it is exactly" but "it is approximately" or "it is like." This word often translates the Hebrew "כְּ" (k', "like") in the Greek texts of the Old Testament.
G5616.emploi: The word appears 21 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels and Acts. It primarily serves to express visual or sensory comparisons: the Spirit descends like a dove (Matthew 3:16), the apostles see tongues of fire (Acts 2:3). It is also systematically used with numbers to express approximation: "about five thousand," "about three thousand" (Luke 9:14; Acts 2:41). It is a word of everyday language, that of narration and eyewitness testimony, which respects the natural imprecision of living narrative.
G5616.portee: This word reminds believers that faith often comes through images and comparisons, not through abstract definitions. When Jesus in agony sweats blood, or when the Spirit descends like a dove, these are appearances that reveal spiritual reality. It also teaches us honesty: the apostles do not claim to know the exact number of converts, but give the order of magnitude. It is a sobriety in testimony.

sens: Prophet of Israel in the 8th century B.C.
G5617.detail: Hosea is a prophet of the Old Testament, sent by God to the northern kingdom (Israel) in the 8th century B.C. His name means "salvation" in Hebrew. He is the author of the prophetic book that bears his name, in which he announces God's judgment on Israel because of its unfaithfulness, but also divine restoration and forgiveness. Paul quotes him in Romans 9:25 to show that God calls to Himself peoples who were once rejected, thus fulfilling Hosea's promise.
G5617.origine: His Hebrew name הוֹשֵׁעַ (Hoshéa) means "salvation" or "he who saves." It is a theophoric name, expressing trust in God the Savior. Hosea lived in the 8th century B.C. during the reigns of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah of Judah, and under Jeroboam II and his successors in Israel.
G5617.emploi: Hosea is mentioned only once in the New Testament, in Romans 9:25, where the Apostle Paul quotes the book of the prophet to illustrate the mystery of the inclusion of the Gentiles in the people of God. Paul applies Hosea's word — that God calls "beloved" those who were not beloved — to the situation of the Gentiles integrated into the Church. This quotation shows that salvation in Jesus Christ fulfills what the prophets of the Old Testament already announced about God's mercy toward the nations.
G5617.portee: Hosea reminds the Christian reader that God never abandons His people despite their unfaithfulness, and that His grace extends far beyond the borders of Israel. The prophet's quotation in Romans 9 invites the believer to recognize that God's love for each of us — as for those who were once rejected — is free, unmerited, and irrevocable.

sens: In the same way as, with the same modality
Exactly or precisely in the same manner
A resemblance or a comparison between two realities
An equality or parity of condition or effect
G5618.detail:
1. The word introduces a direct comparison: it shows that two things happen in the same way. For example, in Matthew 6:2, the hypocrites give alms "as" those who want to be seen — that is, they act in the same manner, with the same motive.
2. It often creates a correspondence between a cause and an effect, or between two parallel realities. In Romans 5:19, "for as by one man's disobedience many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous": the two situations mirror each other, with the same structure and scope.
3. It can express a vivid similarity or a striking image. In Matthew 24:27, the coming of the Son of Man is "as" lightning: it presents the spectacular and sudden image that lights up everything.
G5618.origine: The Greek word ὥσπερ (hōsper) comes from two elements: ὡς (hōs, "as") and περ (per, a particle of reinforcement and generality). This combination gives an intensified "as," with the idea of "just as, exactly as." The word belongs to the family of comparative conjunctions and is similar to the French "ainsi que" or "de même que." In the Greek Septuagint of the Old Testament, it often translates Hebrew comparisons, notably those that begin with כְּ (kə, "as").
G5618.emploi: This comparative word appears 36 times in the New Testament, particularly in Matthew and in Paul's epistles. It is rarely alone: it generally prepares a response introduced by οὕτως ("thus") or by δὲ ("similarly"). In Matthew 12:40, Jesus uses it to compare His resurrection to that of Jonah: "For as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish, so will the Son of Man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth." In 1 Thessalonians 5:3, Paul uses it for a dramatic comparison: destruction will come "as labor pains upon a pregnant woman." Especially in Paul, the word serves to weave theological parallels between the old Adam and Christ, between sin and grace. Its use is therefore both rhetorical (creating images) and doctrinal (establishing correspondences).
G5618.portee: This seemingly transparent word guides the reader in the logic of biblical comparisons. It invites them to see how Scripture functions: it does not describe in isolation, but connects spiritual realities to images and tangible parallels. Understanding ὥσπερ means learning to follow biblical reasoning, where a truth is revealed by its resemblance to another. It is also an invitation to vigilance: when Jesus or Paul say "as," they establish a correspondence that deserves reflection and guides our understanding of the mystery of God.

sens: With an infinitive, expresses the result or consequence of an action
With an indicative verb, introduces a conclusion or direct consequence
Expresses an intention or desired goal
Marks a logical deduction or conclusion
Is equivalent to 'therefore' or 'consequently'
G5620.detail:
1. With an infinitive, the word expresses the result of an action, what naturally follows: 'the storm was so great that it covered the boat with waves' (Matthew 8:24). The emphasis is on the actual or expected effect.
2. When it accompanies an indicative verb, it introduces a conclusion or consequence: 'For God so loved the world that he gave his one and only Son' (John 3:16) — God's love is so great that it resulted in the gift of the Son.
3. Sometimes the word expresses an intention or purpose: 'Jesus gave his disciples the power to drive out evil spirits' so that they might heal the sick (Matthew 10:1) — the result is intended and anticipated.
4. It also serves as a logical marker in reasoning: 'He who marries his daughter does well, but he who does not marry her does better' — therefore, he who does not marry her acts wisely (1 Corinthians 7:38).
5. It can simply equate to 'therefore' or 'consequently' to draw a deduction from the previous verse: 'Therefore, keep watch' (1 Corinthians 4:5) — such is the practical conclusion.
G5620.origine: The word comes from the contraction of two Greek particles: ὡς ('as') and τε ('and'), literally meaning 'and thus'. This combination gradually took on the meaning of a particle of consequence. It belongs to the family of linking particles in ancient Greek, which serve to connect ideas and show their logical relationships.
G5620.emploi: This word appears 83 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels and Paul's epistles. Matthew frequently uses it to describe the spectacular effects of miracles: the storm is so violent that it covers the boat (Matthew 8:24), the crowd gathers to the point that people can no longer find room (Mark 2:2). Paul uses it to develop his theological and practical arguments: 'You have become my people' after the gift of the Spirit (1 Corinthians 3:7), or to state calls to action: 'Work out your own salvation' (Philippians 2:12). The meaning varies slightly depending on the grammatical context (infinitive, indicative, imperative), but the central idea remains: to show how an action or quality produces a consequence.
G5620.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reinforces the cause-and-effect relationship between faith and its fruits, between divine action and human response. When Scripture says 'God loved the world so that he gave his Son', it shows that our salvation is not accidental, but logically follows from God's eternal love. This word also helps to grasp how the miracles of Jesus produce visible and undeniable effects, and how our Christian decisions or attitudes should naturally flow from our faith and lead to practical consequences.

sens: Part of the human body that serves to hear
Ability to listen and understand
Attention to what is said
G5621.detail:
1. The ear is literally the part of the body through which we hear sounds. In the Gospel, Peter cuts off the ear of the servant of the high priest during the arrest of Jesus (Matthew 26:51), and Jesus heals it by touching it (Luke 22:51).
2. The ear also refers to the ability to listen, to receive what is said. It represents the openness of the heart to the word, to teaching, to what God wants to communicate.
3. To have an ear means to pay attention, to be attentive to what is said. It is a call to truly listen, not just to hear sounds, but to grasp the meaning and message.
G5621.origine: The Greek word ōtion is a diminutive of oûs ('ear'). It is a small affectionate or precise word, like when one says 'little ear'. The Hebrew of the Old Testament uses the word ozèn to refer to the ear, which expresses both the physical organ and the act of listening, of paying attention. In the Bible, the ear is not just an organ of hearing: it is a symbol of obedience and receptivity to God.
G5621.emploi: The word ear appears three times in the Gospels, all in the account of the arrest of Jesus. Matthew and John report that Peter cuts off the ear of the servant of the high priest (Matthew 26:51, John 18:26). Luke reports the same event but adds that Jesus heals this ear by touching it (Luke 22:51). These three accounts describe a concrete and dramatic moment: instead of the violence expected by the disciples, Jesus chooses healing and compassion towards an enemy.
G5621.portee: This passage shows that even in the face of evil and betrayal, Jesus responds with healing, not destruction. The severed ear becomes a symbol of rupture and injury; its healing symbolizes the forgiveness and restoration that Jesus brings. It reminds us that the way of Jesus is not violence, but mercy.

sens: What is useful, what serves a purpose
Advantage gained from something
Profit or benefit obtained
What motivates a self-interested action
G5622.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes what is useful, what serves or helps. It is what has a practical function, which can serve to achieve a goal. When Paul asks 'What advantage then is there in being a Jew?' (Romans 3:1), he questions what it concretely means to be Jewish if circumcision does not bring salvation.
2. Usefulness becomes advantage when one calculates what one gains. In Jude 1:16, false teachers admire people 'for the sake of gain', meaning they hope to derive personal profit or material benefit.
3. This word can also refer to the benefit one reaps — the net gain from a situation. It is the idea of what profits us, what enriches or advances us.
G5622.origine: The word comes from a root meaning 'to bear' or 'to produce': it denotes what something produces or brings. The same family contains the verb 'ὠφελέω' (to help, to serve). In Hebrew, this word often translates roots expressing profit or advantage (עַל hi., בְּצַע).
G5622.emploi: The word appears twice in the New Testament. In Romans 3:1, Paul uses it to question the practical advantage of being a Jew in light of justification by faith. In Jude 1:16, he describes false teachers who flatter the rich out of pure self-interest, to gain profit from them. The context always shows a reflection on what 'pays off' or what 'benefits'.
G5622.portee: This word invites us to examine our true motivations: do we act out of genuine interest for God and others, or out of personal profit and material interest? As Jude denounces, selfish interest perverts faith by turning it into a tool for gain. Paul's question in Romans 3 also reminds us that no human advantage — status, wealth, merit — saves us: only God's grace justifies us.

sens: Be useful, bring an advantage or profit
Assist someone, do a service for them or help them
Produce no result, be ineffective
G5623.detail:
1. The fundamental meaning is "to be useful" or "to benefit someone." It is the idea that an action or thing produces a beneficial effect: it helps, it advances, it improves the situation. Thus, Pilate sees that he "gains nothing" by discussing with the crowd (Matthew 27:24), meaning that it serves him no purpose, does not help him.
2. The word can also mean "to assist," "to provide help to someone." Jesus reproaches the Pharisees for denying parents the support (the assistance) that children could have given them by pretending it is an offering to God (Matthew 15:5). To assist here means "to take care of, to support."
3. In its negative form, the word expresses ineffectiveness, the absence of profit: "What does it serve?", "It is of no use!" Luke 9:25 asks: "What would it profit a man to gain the whole world if he loses himself?" — that is, what good is it? What profit, what advantage?
G5623.origine: The word comes from the Greek root ὄφελος ("profit," "advantage"), which evokes the idea of growth or benefit. The verbal form ὠφελέω ("serve to," "benefit") has retained this idea of producing a useful result. It is a common word in Greek to express practical utility and real gain. In the Greek Old Testament, it often translates the Hebrew יָעַל ("to be useful," "to serve"), showing that both languages express the same notion: an act that produces a concrete good.
G5623.emploi: The verb appears 15 times in the New Testament, mainly in Matthew and Mark. It is first used with an accusative ("serve to someone"): assisting a parent is "serving to him" by supporting him (Matthew 15:5). It is also used in the passive, notably in Hebrews 13:9, where it is said that certain practices "are of no use." The verb often takes a negative turn: "gain nothing" (Matthew 27:24, John 12:19), "serve nothing" (1 Corinthians 13:3). Finally, it can express a worried doubt: "What does it serve?" (Luke 9:25, Mark 8:36). In all cases, it questions the real utility, the true profit of an action or possession.
G5623.portee: This word invites the Christian reader to examine what is truly useful for their life and salvation. It highlights a central question: What "serves what" in my life? The accumulation of wealth, success, religious practices — do they really serve any purpose if I lose my soul? Jesus precisely asks: "What would it profit to gain the whole world and lose oneself?" He calls to redefine true profit: what matters is salvation and the relationship with God, not illusory earthly advantages.

sens: That which produces an advantage, a practical benefit
That which serves a purpose, which has utility
That which deserves to be put into practice
G5624.detail:
1. A word that designates what brings profit, a concrete fruit. When Paul says that "bodily exercise is of little profit" (1 Timothy 4:8), he means that physical fitness provides us with a limited benefit: it is a measurable and concrete improvement, but minor.
2. That which has a function, a practical value — that which we need because it serves a purpose. Godliness, on the other hand, is "useful for everything": it fulfills its function for all areas of life, preparing us to receive both the goods of this world and those of the world to come.
3. That which deserves to be applied and implemented. Scripture is "useful for teaching, for reproof, for correction, for instruction" (2 Timothy 3:16): it is good to take, good to use, capable of producing these results in those who listen to it.
G5624.origine: The word comes from the root "ōphélé," which means "profit" or "advantage" (hence also the verb "ōphéléô," to be useful, to benefit). It is a matter of practical utility, of real benefit. In Hebrew, similar words are found to express the idea of use, application, of what truly serves.
G5624.emploi: The word appears only three times in the New Testament, always in the pastoral epistles (1 and 2 Timothy, Titus). Paul uses it to compare what is truly worth the effort. In 1 Timothy 4:8, he relativizes sports in relation to godliness: both are "useful," but to very different degrees. In 2 Timothy 3:16, Scripture itself is declared useful — not as a mere interesting book, but as an active tool for transforming those who receive it. In Titus 3:8, in a slightly different context ("good works"), the idea remains one of utility that deserves our commitment.
G5624.portee: This word reminds the Christian of practical wisdom: to evaluate what is truly worth investing time and energy in. Paul poses the direct question — is it really useful? — to help us prioritize our commitments. Godliness, Scripture, good works are not spiritual luxuries: they are profitable investments. The word calls for a faith that is not dreamy, but fruitful.

sens: In the same way as, also as
Introduces a comparison or an approximate resemblance
Expresses a similarity while marking a certain reservation or attenuation
G5619.detail:
1. The word introduces a direct comparison: it brings two things or situations closer by saying they resemble each other. In 1 Corinthians 15:8, Paul compares his experience of meeting the risen Christ to that of the other apostles — he had a vision, "as" they had.
2. It can soften or nuance the comparison, as if saying "in a way" or "so to speak." Here, Paul suggests that his experience is similar to that of the apostles, but he does not assert it absolutely: it occurs late, "as to one untimely born," which marks a certain exception or difference.
3. The word serves to make accessible a reality that is difficult to describe by relating it to something known.
G5619.origine: The Greek word is composed of ὡς ("as") and an ancient form of expression. It belongs to the family of comparative words, frequently used in Greek to establish comparisons. This expressive structure is typical of biblical Greek.
G5619.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Corinthians 15:8. Paul uses it to describe his personal encounter with the risen Christ. He asserts that, although he came after the other apostles and compares himself to "one untimely born," he indeed received a revelation of the risen Lord, "as" the others did. This pivotal passage raises the question of Paul's apostolic legitimacy and the assurance of his calling.
G5619.portee: For the Christian reader, this passage reminds us that a personal experience of meeting Christ can be as real and decisive as that of the great apostles, even if it occurs differently or later. It is a word of encouragement for all those who doubt the validity of their own calling or their own experience with God. Paul affirms that Christ can reveal Himself in a living and transformative way, to each according to His grace.
